summary: We have developed a web application that helps you plan your routes through Mars, taking into account the maximum slope percentage, the maximum autonomy and speed and the time needed between rests. There is an example route made for studying volcanoes having taken into account the proximity of the volcanoes and the zone of the base, which is shielded from radiation.
details:
Marswalk is an interactive route planning tool that brings Martian terrain, scientific objectives and mission timing into one application.

What it does and how it works

Users select the prepared itinerary or create a custom route by placing points on a map. Each point can represent a science station, rest stop, proposed landing area, habitat or communications checkpoint.

Marswalk retrieves NASA MOLA elevation data and uses Dijkstra’s algorithm to connect destinations in their selected order while respecting a configurable sampled-slope limit. It calculates travel time from walking speed, adds activity durations and automatically proposes rest stops. Users can include a return journey and reserve part of their autonomy on return.

The same itinerary appears across topographic and satellite views, helping users understand where they are placing the points of interest. Each point includes its purpose, arrival time and available terrain context. Plans can be exported as GeoJSON with their scientific references.

Benefits and intended impact

Marswalk makes dispersed scientific information easier to explore together. Users can see how changing destinations, walking speed, activity time or reserve affects the complete mission—including its return journey.

Its intended impact is educational and exploratory: helping students understand the trade-offs involved in planning human surface exploration.

Tools and development

The project was developed using Python and Streamlit, with JavaScript, HTML, CSS and Leaflet powering the interactive map. NumPy and pandas support numerical calculations and mission tables; Matplotlib generates topographic shading and contours; Plotly displays interactive charts; and Requests and Pillow handle data access and imagery.

GitHub provides source hosting, and Streamlit Community Cloud hosts the public application. Development also used OpenAI Codex for coding, testing and debugging. Automated tests check route behaviour, rest scheduling, terrain rendering and environmental-data handling. The application runs in a web browser without specialised hardware.

What makes it creative

Marswalk combines a route planner with a scientific field itinerary. Numbered points connect the map, elevation profile, activities and source data, allowing users to inspect a mission from several perspectives without losing its geographic context.

Its premade mission has been prepared to study multiple volcanoes close apart, and minimizing radiation in the base.

Factors considered

We considered usability, data availability, terrain resolution and the distinction between simulation and operational planning. The interface keeps advanced settings folded away while preserving access to sources, observation dates and calculation assumptions.

Safety-related limitations are explicit. Coarse elevation data cannot resolve rocks, fissures or sand hazards; resting does not necessarily replenish autonomy; and historical weather or detector measurements cannot certify future conditions. Marswalk is a planning prototype, not a certified astronaut-navigation or safety system.
